best_for: Python developers who want a full IDE with refactoring and Jupyter built in, and who will decide after the trial whether Pro's extras are worth a subscription.

points.title: One app, free core
points.text: Since 2025.1 PyCharm is a single product. The core features, now including Jupyter notebooks, stay free; a Pro subscription adds the advanced tools. New installs start with a 30-day Pro trial.

points.title: When the trial ends
points.text: You choose: buy Pro, or keep using the free core features. Existing Professional licenses keep full access with no change.

points.title: It wants a strong machine
points.text: JetBrains lists a 4-core x86_64 or arm64 CPU, 8 GB of RAM with 3 GB free for the IDE, 10 GB of disk and a 1280 by 720 screen.

points.title: Supported systems
points.text: Windows 10 and 11, macOS 26 and 27, and Linux with glibc 2.28 or newer, tested on Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, Fedora 44 and 45, Debian 13 and Amazon Linux 2023. BSD is not supported.

points.title: Remote work over SSH
points.text: Remote development needs OpenSSH 7.9p1 or later on the server and a local or block disk; network shares such as NFS and SMB are not supported.

points.title: Windows install, your choice
points.text: The Windows installer can install per user or for the whole machine, in x64 and Arm64 builds. Macs get separate Intel and Apple silicon builds. The Windows listing keeps 34 versions; macOS and Linux list only the current release.

points.title: Linux lags here
points.text: The Linux listing is a Flathub build, not marked verified, at 2026.2.2 while Windows and macOS are on 2026.3.0.1. For the newest Linux build, use JetBrains' own download.
